channel.title: Pier — Blog
channel.description: Practical writing on legacy websites, FTP, MySQL and AI-assisted edits.

item.title: Backups that aren't really backups: a seven-point audit
item.description: An agency lead sent a Loom at 23:41: the restore file was 11 MB, the database is 4.7 GB. Here's how that happens, and how to make sure it doesn't to you.
item.dc:creator: Pier editorial

item.title: Inline CSS and embedded fonts: 2010s habits that aged well
item.description: Eleven years on, the parts of a 2014 WordPress theme still doing useful work are the ones we used to mock: inline CSS, self-hosted fonts, plain JavaScript.
item.dc:creator: Pier editorial

item.title: Shared cPanel clients: the four kinds and what they need
item.description: Most agency portfolios still have a shared cPanel tail. Four kinds of clients live on it, and spotting which one is in front of you shortens the rest of the conversation.
item.dc:creator: Pier editorial

item.title: Legacy PHP site snapshot: a one-afternoon playbook
item.description: You just got handed SFTP creds, a vague Slack thread, and a site nobody has touched in four years. Here is how to know what you are looking at by 5pm.
item.dc:creator: Pier editorial

item.title: Composer and the legacy PHP site you just inherited
item.description: You inherited a WordPress install with three plugins, three vendored Guzzles, and zero composer.json. Composer init is the wrong first move. Here is the audit that comes first.
item.dc:creator: Pier editorial

item.title: Magento 1 in 2026: editing live without nuking the catalog cache
item.description: A Dutch agency, a frozen Magento 1 shop, a Friday at 23:41, and the catalog_product_flat tables that nearly took the storefront down at checkout time.
item.dc:creator: Pier editorial

item.title: Public web root: seven file types you should never expose
item.description: A WordPress install live since 2014 will tell you everything about itself if you know which seven files to ask for. None of them should be there.
item.dc:creator: Pier editorial

item.title: AI-assisted PHP review: what it catches, what it misses
item.description: An honest look at what AI code review actually changes when you're refactoring 14-year-old PHP: the bugs it finds in seconds, the legacy decisions it can't read.
item.dc:creator: Pier editorial

item.title: Front-controller routing: why /contact is not contact.php
item.description: The contact page on a 12-year-old WordPress site shows a 500 error. The first instinct is to open contact.php in FTP. That file does not exist, and it never did.
item.dc:creator: Pier editorial

item.title: Drupal 7 end-of-life: a checklist for clients still on it
item.description: Drupal 7 went unsupported in January 2025. The sites still humming along on it in mid-2026 are not unsupported by accident, they are unsupported by neglect.
item.dc:creator: Pier editorial

item.title: WordPress MySQL queries: a legacy maintainer's cheatsheet
item.description: The half-dozen SQL statements that fix legacy WordPress sites at 17:40 on a Tuesday: URL pair, autoload audit, revisions purge, password reset, transient sweep.
item.dc:creator: Pier editorial

item.title: FTP is not dead: when SFTP is overkill and FTPS is just right
item.description: A Friday hotfix on a Magento 1 site, no SSH, no port 22 open, and the question gets suddenly real. SFTP is not always the answer, and FTPS is not the compromise it gets framed as.

item.title: wp-config.php on production: a safe edit procedure

item.title: Joomla migration without SEO loss: a 12-year-old case study
item.description: A 12-year-old Joomla 2.5 site, three SEF plugins deep, moving to PHP 8.2 hosting. Here's how the redirects, the database, and the rankings survived the week.

item.title: Legacy PHP reinfection: the .htaccess wall that holds
